meta.title: What AI Agents Need to Actually Work | The Next Endeavor 2026
meta.speakers: Liran Zvibel (WEKA), Satyen Sangani (Alation), Melissa Valentine (Stanford), plus an unnamed moderator
meta.thread_line: 4 threads · evals as the bottom layer · catalogs and who owns meaning · storage after the warehouse · agent-first adoption and security

snapshot: Panel on the unglamorous layer under enterprise agents: evals, data catalogs, storage and ownership.
Consensus: **evals** are the hardest and most under-estimated part; agents checking agents still bottom out in human-built ground truth.
Production agents drift: data schemas, business rules and tool versions all change after launch, so every fix raises a knowledge-management question.
A catalog is an inventory of what *is*; agents need what *ought to be*, defined per use case, with owners from technical, functional and content roles.
Storage view: warehouses and SQL were built for humans; two panelists expect a return to a data lake with vector plus graph on top, but nobody claims a settled answer.
Agent-first design and in-house inference are driven by access control: each user's credentials must follow every nested agent call.
A bank case study reached about 99% agentic resolution and now struggles with the 1% of edge cases and with organizational trust.

themes.title: Evals are the bottom turtle, and drift keeps breaking them
themes.lead: Loops of agents checking agents still rest on verified, human-created eval data, and that layer is the hardest to build.
bullets: Valentine's answer to what firms underestimate was "hands down evals": defining success well enough to create ground truth is tedious and people hate doing it.
She borrowed the phrase "turtles all the way down" from an Arize developer: loops upon loops of agents, with evals at the bottom.
Sangani: stochastic apps *drift*. Data schemas, context, business rules and tool versions change, so a failing eval forces a triage between knowledge base, data quality, access or prompt.
Each fix raises a scope question: is the corrected truth global or true only for this use case, and which container holds it.
Zvibel: a year ago the obsession was hallucination; with reasoning models and good starting context it rarely appears now.
The new failure is nested agents answering from different understandings of context; each step is logical but the end result looks ridiculous to a human, so verify what every stage feeds the next.

quote.text: At the bottom of all of those loops of agents checking agents checking agents is you have to have a really nice layer of verified, typically human created data of evals.

names.name: Arize
names.blurb: Startup whose developer coined the 'turtles all the way down' eval framing; named as an example by Valentine

themes.title: A catalog is a map of what is, and ownership spans three roles
themes.lead: Agent-ready context is defined by the use case and the eval, and owned jointly by technical, functional and content people.
bullets: Sangani: a catalog describes what *is*; a messy catalog is a map of messy data, and agents need what *ought to be*.
Building "context" in isolation is the wrong target; you cannot know when you are done without a defined use case and eval.
Ownership in an agentic world needs a technical individual, a functional individual and a content owner: three people or thirty.
Zvibel: no enterprise project is truly AI-first since the mess predates agents; the realistic move is to modernize the data, with flash instead of hard drives for low latency.
Valentine's 2021 course research found the data-scientist and domain-expert relationship was the top predictor of effective ML; she now sees forward-deployed engineers filling that role for GenAI.
Her bank site hit about 99% agentic resolution; the workforce lacks expertise for the gnarly 1% and the bank is stuck on building trust across legal, HR and compliance to launch new use cases faster.
themes.watch: Sangani sells a data catalog and Zvibel sells storage, so both are describing the layer their own products occupy.

themes.title: Storage after the warehouse: data lake, vector and graph
themes.lead: SQL and warehouses were designed for humans; panelists lean toward a lake with semantic search on top but admit the end state is unclear.
bullets: Sangani: religion about one architecture is damaging; he cited Iceberg table formats decoupling compute from storage and prefers "different horses for different courses".
Alation is releasing an ontology product built with agents; the promise is that users just declare intent and things happen.
Zvibel: SQL lets smart humans translate wishes into what a schema supports; he has a strong hunch that is not the AI-native way, and models hold far more context than one person.
His prediction: the industry returns toward a data lake on a vector store, with a small agent massaging the prompt and distilling results, though he has no "silver bullet" yet.

Q&A: a former JPMorgan data lead (now running a financial AI-workforce startup) suggested everything ends in a file system with vector search, citing LanceDB; Zvibel agreed storage ends up closer to a file system with semantic search, plus a graph.
The audience also raised temporal drift: an agent asked about yesterday at 10:00 must know that day's truth, not today's.
themes.watch: Zvibel says the situation hasn't stabilized and he hasn't seen the end result; this is a hunch, not a finding.

names.name: WEKA
names.blurb: Storage vendor; Zvibel's company, supplying dense, low-latency file storage to GPU clouds

themes.title: Agent-first companies and why security pulls inference in-house
themes.lead: Both vendors rebuilt themselves around agents, and credential propagation is pushing large enterprises to run their own stack.
bullets: WEKA started 13 years ago building a low-latency file system; early big customers in 2017 were GPU users, and the GPT moment turned a detour into the core business.
Zvibel: engineers used coding agents for a year-plus, then after a December-January inflection the whole company moved to AI; systems without an MCP get one built in-house.
WEKA embeds the equivalent of forward-deployed engineers; HR, finance and go-to-market now run hundreds of dashboards, agents and automated processes.
For sensitive data WEKA moved to its own GPUs, inference and internal MCPs, which controls who sees what and lets them open everything to AI.

Sangani: every data read or write will be intermediated by an agent, so Alation designed for agents first two years ago and bought Numbers Station, a Stanford-PhD team applying transformers to structured data.

Zvibel: user A's and user B's credentials must follow the whole nested agent chain, and a blanket-access API call to a cloud model doesn't work; this pushes large enterprises to bring infrastructure in-house.
themes.watch: Both operator accounts come from vendors selling into this market.

takeaways.title: Budget for human-built eval data first; treat agent-checks-agent loops as a layer on top of it.
Plan for drift: schemas, rules and tool versions change, so every failed eval needs a triage path to the right fix.
Define context per use case and eval, not as a standalone catalog project.
Pair a technical owner, a functional owner and a content owner on every agentic process.
Check that each user's credentials follow every nested agent call before opening data to agents.
Stay architecture-agnostic on warehouse, lake, vector and graph; fit storage to the use case.

hot_takes.take: It's actually so... hands down evals.
hot_takes.why: names evals the most underestimated factor

hot_takes.take: A warehouse or any SQL database is something that was created for humans... we have a strong hunch that this is not the AI native way to hold data for the models.
I think the end is going to be a lot closer to going back to a data lake.
Context in isolation is sort of a silly thing to go after, because how do you even know you're done?
I wouldn't call any of these projects AI-first, because the mess was created for a long, long time.

claims.claim: Enterprise data storage returns toward a data lake on a vector store, with agents doing the semantic work.
claims.target: data lake plus vector store (and graph)

other_news.title: Sources referenced: an Arize YouTube video (eval 'turtles' quote), Valentine's 2021 Stanford class 'Managing Data Science Organizations', and LanceDB (audience question).
Valentine runs embedded research sites with PhD students, watching how AI is implemented inside companies and with what impact.

glossary.def: Verified, typically human-created test data that defines what a correct agent output looks like.
Gradual change in data schemas, business rules, context or tool versions that breaks a previously working stochastic app.
A company-internal 'Wikipedia for data': an inventory describing the data an organization has.
A technical builder embedded with domain experts to gain enough business context to build a working system.
Open table format that separates compute from storage, giving companies flexibility and sovereignty.
Model Context Protocol, the connector standard that lets agents reach internal systems.
